- If sentiment is consistently 0.00, model tends to overestimate early in the horizon and underestimates later — adjust forecast to flatten upward slope after initial spike.
- If sentiment is >0.00 (even low), model often overreacts to recent highs, leading to overshoot — reduce forecast peak by 2–5% relative to immediate prior value.
- When true outcome shows sharp upward move (e.g., >5% from prior), model often fails to capture it — increase forecast sensitivity to recent 3–5 day mean reversion.
- If model forecast is flat or slowly rising while true outcome shows volatility, model underestimates mean reversion — add 1–3% upward bias to forecast for 3–5 days after volatility spike.
- If sentiment is 0.00 and model forecast is rising steadily, true outcome often reverses — reduce forecast slope by 1–2% per day after 5 days of upward trend.
- For 30-day horizon, model often misses late-period spikes — add 1–3% upward bias to final 5–7 days if sentiment is 0.00 and recent 7-day mean is rising.
